messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I am working at the moment on a 3 year project, trying to estimate an ungulate population in a forested area. And I got some question related to my density estimations; I would really appreciate some help!!

Shortly to the setup of my study:  10 line-transects (each transect 50 to 60 km Length). Fieldwork is done every year in summer (August-Sept) and in spring/winter (Febr-March). In the summer we do our sampling twice on each transect (10 transect *2 = 20 nights), in winter we sample each transect three times (10 transects * 3= 30 nights). We are sampling with the help of 2 infrared- cameras from a car driving on forest paths (forest paths were chosen randomly and the habitat along transects are representative for the area, cameras are installed left and right hand side of the car). Our survey area is a low-mountain region (400 – 670m of elevation) with a dense, deeply incised system of valleys and wide variety of hill shapes, which makes sampling not always that easy. For this reason and to reduce bias between transects we did additional data acquisition.

The plan of this setup was to see the effect of an introduced predator on the prey population and additionally differences between the two seasons within the prey population. In general we know that we have a higher density in the summer than in the winter (in the autumn hunting season starts, which lasts until end of January – therefore definitive smaller population in winter). But until now our data shows that the first summer (So15) and the first winter (Wi16) have approx. the same density estimation.

CDS

Label                              Estimate          se                 cv                    lcl                     ucl                df

So15 Hn 20m steps     5.958602   1.06185   0.1782042   4.017750   8.837020    9.972106

Wi16 Hn 20m steps     5.876205   1.00951   0.1717969   4.015444   8.599243    9.855644

So16 Hn 20m steps     4.972349   0.75928   0.1527014   3.554515   6.955731   10.607468

Sample sizes in the different seasons:

                Summer 2015:  n= 433

                Winter 2016:     n=670   ( 3 times sampling per transect)

                Summer 2016:   n=415

Is it possible, that even though with a much higher population in summer, that we can´t register the differences due to high vegetation (leaves, bushes etc.?), on the other hand in winter better sightings due to less foliation are possible– so therefore a better estimation? Leads us at the end up to the same population estimate?? Does somebody have experience with comparing two seasons with each other?
If we assume that the Vegetation would play a strong role in our data acquisition then this would not agree with the assumptions of distance: "Distance allow for the fact that many objects will remain undetetected, as Long as they are not on the line or Point.  ... it seems unnecessary to research the influence of these environmental variables ... "

We registered also for each detection the according habitat, running a MCDS does still give us the same results for summer (So15) and winter (Wi16).
Can somebody give some advice ?
Thanks upfront!!

Carolin

messages.body_plain:
Carolin

I can only speculate on possible explanations for the patterns you have provided.

The number of detections per survey you provide at the end of your email suggests you detect ~220 deer on each of your 10-transect visits, regardless of season.  The shapes of the histograms you provide suggest the shape of a detection function is likely to be similar between the 3 surveys.  On the basis of those bits of information, it is not surprising the density estimates are quite similar.

I trust your analysis accounted for the difference in effort (~55km X 10 X #visits) between the seasons.

Recognise also the duration of your surveys, 20-30 nights, is not consistent with the idea of a closed population; in effect, you are estimating the average of the deer population in the study area during the 20-30 days it takes to complete your seasonal survey.

Use of the forest tracks in your sampling protocol causes me to wonder if there may be a seasonal difference affinity for the tracks.  I'm veering dangerously into the realm of biological speculation.  Could it be that your study animals find the region of the tracks more conducive to locomotion or feeding in the winter than in the summer; are the tracks located at lower elevations?  If so (speculation), density in the study area may be lower in winter, but density in area surveyed may not change between seasons.   Additional information about the seasonal spatial use by the study animals (via telemetry) would be a way to eliminate that possible explanation for your findings.

It is this sort of possible confounding of animal density and animal distribution that causes us to caution against placing survey effort in locations that are discernable to the study animals (tracks, headlands, fence rows, etc.).  Here is an excerpt from Buckland et al. (2015) Section 10.5.1

As I said, many of my comments are speculative.

Hi Eric,

thanks for the quick response.
You are right, deer observed per 1 round (10 transects) are quite similar. I also considered the effort according to the visits (I pooled the detections for transect X and multiplied the effort by number of visits).

We discussed the influence of the forestry paths before, but we did not really come to a good conclusion. Due to such a large study area we are almost forced to take the forest paths. To be sure that we don't have a self-made bias in our transects we checked the transects according to elevation and habitat. We found that the transects were representative to the surrounding forestry districts and the total study area. In addition to that we analysed with the help of data from a photo-trap monitoring the spatial use of the deer in respect to the forest paths (study area: two forest habitats closed by to our study area). We found no correlation between the path network, its frequency of use and the spatial use of the deer in the area. That supported our idea of using forestry paths for our survey. On the other hand we use forest roads which consist out of gravel (nutrient input) and dirt roads (without any nutrient input). But maybe exactly the combination of nutrient input and light intensity on the roads could make the roads to a more attractive habitat than the surrounding.  I guess we need to make further investigations on that.

Thanks for your support !!!

Carolin

This is an issue that has come up several times on the Distance list (most recently in 2012) and is discussed in the Distance users guide, in the Appendix called 'Program Reference' under 'Preferences Dialog.'

This is because Distance tries to compress these results, and the compression algorithm does not work with various Asian character sets.  There is a way to fix this:  Under 'Tools' on the menu, select Preferences.  On the tab marked 'General' untick the box labelled 'Store results in compressed format in project databases'  This will prevent the use of compression software that alters Chinese/Japanese/Korean languages.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

You're probably considered these alternatives and rejected them for various reasons, but in case it's useful to you or others:

1. You could do a series of point transects along the roads -- if you can assume the detection function is the same in every direction then it's possible to disentangle density gradient from detection function.  Another bright idea of Tiago's (Marques et al. 2010.  Point transect sampling along linear features.  Biometrics 66: 1247-1255).  It's a bit inefficient though, as you're not surveying between points, plus animal movement can be a problem, as can the assumption of radially symmetric detection function.

2. You could do a double-observer sampling protocol -- i.e., mark-recapture distance sampling.  One does not necessarily need to assume a constant density gradient in the analysis (this is likely documented in the MRDS chapter in the 2004 Advanced Distance Sampling book -- I don't have it to hand).  But double observer protocol is harder to do in practice; plus one needs to assume detections between observer teams are independent (or at least one-way independence) given covariates.

3. Depending on how wide your transects are with respect to the size of the study area, it might be able to fit a density surface model to estimate detectability and density surface at the same time.  Will only work if transects are wide, study area relatively small and (I suspect) density varies quite smoothly; also better if transects are not all parallel.

4. Find another way to survey the animals that doesn't involve surveying on roads!

:)  Len

messages.subject_clean: Stratification - same sample point but stratum differs per observation
messages.body_plain:
I have point count data from a single site and am contemplating using a soil layer as a proxy for habitat conditions. This would be used as a stratum to estimate density and abundance for a single species, preferably across several years.

The easiest thing to do would be to assign every observation with the soil type found at the point count station; however, individuals may, and often times were, using a different soil/stratum away from the survey location. Therefore, it would be more appropriate to assign the soil type that was actually estimated to have been used by the bird.

My questions are:
Will having observations from the same point, in the same year or regardless, but with different strata pose any problems when analyzing the data, especially if I also want to obtain a global estimate across years? However...
According to the 6.2 User Manual, only one level of stratification can occur with both CDS and MCDS.  Focusing for now just on CDS, am I correct in assuming then that I won't be able to obtain estimates per strata and year? Will I need to run each separately and use the mean of stratum-specific density estimates? Or...
Would I be better off using Year as the stratum, then use the resulting density estimates*area of soil type available at the site?
Thanks in advance for any attempts to help. I apologize if this has been addressed elsewhere or if my lack of experience has obscured obvious answers.

John/list:

You've done considerable research, and I don't think your question has an obvious answer.  A partial way forward for you is to record soil layer in the observation layer of your data and post-stratify by soil layer in your analysis; treating soil layer as if it was something like bird sex--could not be ascertained at the time the survey was designed.  However, as you indicate you can have only a single level of stratification in your analyses.

Venturing away from the specifics of the software, I have some scepticism about gathering data for your proposed soil layer analysis.  I have no knowledge about the ecological system you are studying, but your proposed approach presumes

- there are multiple soil layers available for detection in most/all of your points,

- you have a detailed map of soil layers,

- you can localise the bird sighting/song not just to distance from point, but to an (x,y) coordinate

- the accuracy of your bird localisation is sufficient that you can accurately attribute sightings to soil type (if you cannot do this, you will not be estimating what you set out to estimate (soil-specific densities))

The other challenge with post-stratified analyses is the potential that your soil layer distribution relative to your counting stations locations is not uniform.  Unless you have lots of point, by chance it could be the case that soil layer A is never closer than 100m to any of your stations, whereas soil layer B is never further than 75m from any counting station.  To make progress with your proposition, I suggest you assess the distribution of soil types with respect to your counting stations, before going further.

If this is a study yet-to-be conducted, and the patch size of soil layers permit, considering designing your survey so as to treat soil layer explicitly in your survey design.

Katy

You get style points for ingenuity trying to build a density surface model, but you are taking the long way around.

You can indeed fit a detection function to binned data using ddf().  Examples of such an analysis is provided under

?ddf
# simulated double observer point count data (see ?ptdata.dual)
# setup data
data(ptdata.dual)
ptdata.dual$distbegin <- (as.numeric(cut(ptdata.dual$distance,10*(0:10)))-1)*10
ptdata.dual$distend <- (as.numeric(cut(ptdata.dual$distance,10*(0:10))))*10

model <- ddf(method="io", data=ptdata.dual, dsmodel=~cds(key="hn"),
             mrmodel=~glm(formula=~distance*observer),
             meta.data=list(point=TRUE, binned=TRUE, breaks=10*(0:10)))

summary(model)

Note this example is of point count data, but the idea is to create $distbegin and $distend fields
in your data, then specify in "meta.data" binned=TRUE and breaks= for the breakpoints.

Ask again if you need further help with the binning.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm currently trying to generate sample-level density estimates from a set of point counts where each point was visited 3 times, each time by a different observer. I've gone though the model selection process and have settled on one model (MCDS with hazard rate key, simple polynomial adjustment, and observer as a covariate) that by all measures seems to be the best model and has good fit. However, when I go to generate sample-level density estimates for this model, my resulting density/abundance estimates seem to be occurring at discrete intervals (i.e. 9, 18, 27, etc) rather than along a continuous range.

I found an older posting asking essentially the same question here:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/sample$20level$20density%7Csort:relevance/distance-sampling/2XA2SkjT2ak/xYAYKqStp5IJ

Based on the recommendations from this posting I've made sure that my model specifies only "sample" for the level of resolution for the density estimate, and that both "sample" and "global" are checked for the detection function, however my resulting density estimates are still occurring in discrete intervals. As a comparison I've tried generating point-specific density estimates from other models (both CDS and MCDS) and still get density estimates occurring only in intervals.

Am I still doing something wrong in trying to estimate point-specific densities, and if not can anyone explain why I'm not getting a continuous range of density estimates?

Thanks,
Nathaniel Behl

M.S. student, Benkman Lab
Department of Zoology & Physiology
University of Wyoming

Nathaniel

Sorry I didn't answer this when you originally posted the question in mid-January.

The explanation for the abundance estimates you observed has to do with the nature of transect-level estimate.  Estimates for each of your points is simply the number of detections at that point scaled up by dividing count by probability of detection.

The example you so helpfully provided "my abundance estimates seem to be occurring at discrete intervals (i.e. 9, 18, 27, etc)" made it easy to deduce that via your fitted detection function, the estimated probability of detecting a bird (given it is within the truncation distance of the point) was 0.11.

Therefore, at points where there was a single detection, the estimate of abundance is 9 (1/0.11); points were there were two detections had an estimated abundance of 18 (2/0.11), etc.  Because you have observer as a covariate, the divisor would differ for points sampled by different observers.

Producing estimates at the scale of the point transect washes out replication that would produce a more continuous range of estimates.

point transect data (transect="point") when running your model, not
currently featured in any examples on the website (though I am working

cheers,

Eric Rexstad recently helped me follow up on my original question regarding cluster size bias using observation team as a covariate (with a total of 10 different teams). I'd like to share this off-list exchange since posting my original question in case others have the same issue.
